slides.title: The Cost of the Critical Path
slides.alt: The Cost of the Critical Path:
slides.transcript: This module changes the goal from the cut to delay: the longest path delay of a combinational circuit. Each crossing between clusters adds a fixed delay D to the path, and one logic node may be copied into several clusters. Note: this submission is Lesson 9, while Lab 09 in the teacher’s catalogue is Multilevel; the correspondence awaits confirmation.

slides.title: The goal has changed: from cut to delay
slides.alt: The goal has changed: from cut to delay: Chain P→X→Y→O: δ = 1, inter-cluster D = 3, capacity 2; {P,X} | {Y,O}: 1 crossing, delay 7; {P} | {X,Y} | {O}: 2 crossings, delay 10; Delay follows how often the critical path crosses a boundary
slides.transcript: Start with a chain. Both splits respect the capacity, but the first crosses a boundary once, delay 7; the second crosses twice, delay 10. Delay depends only on how many boundaries the longest path crosses, not on how many wires are cut in total.

slides.title: The RW model
slides.alt: The RW model: A combinational DAG; PIs are inputs, POs outputs; Node delay δ(v); 0 on wires inside a cluster, D between; Cluster capacity M (the sum of node sizes); Logic nodes may be replicated; Goal: minimise the largest PI→PO delay
slides.transcript: The RW model is a directed acyclic graph. Each node has a delay, wires inside a cluster add none, wires between clusters add a fixed D, each cluster has a capacity, and nodes may be replicated. The goal is to minimise the largest delay from input to output.

slides.title: Replication: logic nodes and instances
slides.alt: Replication: logic nodes and instances: One logic node (logicalId) may have several physical instances (instanceId); An instance is written “node@root”; Replication lets several clusters get the same signal inside; The cost: every copy takes area; A “node → cluster” map cannot express replication
slides.transcript: Replication puts the same logic node into several clusters; each copy is an instance. It lets several clusters get the same signal from inside, but every copy takes area. As data, logic nodes and instances must be recorded separately.

slides.title: Initialisation: the candidate DAG and Δ
slides.alt: Initialisation: the candidate DAG and Δ: The original 12-node example: PIs a, b, c; POs k, l; δ = 1, D = 3, capacity 4; Δ(x, v): the longest node delay from x to v (counting v, not x); Δ(b, k) = 4 (b→e→g→i→k); The graph is reconstructed from the original film: candidate data
slides.transcript: The original 12-node example is reconstructed from frames of the film. Δ is the longest node delay from x to v, counting v but not x; for example from b to k it is 4. This graph is candidate data; the original edge list awaits the original author’s confirmation.

slides.title: Labelling: l(v) = max(l1, l2)
slides.alt: Labelling: l(v) = max(l1, l2): Score(x) = l(x) + Δ(x, v); Candidate cluster: v + the highest-scoring ancestors, up to capacity; Ties: the later in topological order (this course’s assumption); l1 = largest score of a PI inside; l2 = largest score outside + D; i: l1 = 4, l2 = 7 → l(i) = 7
slides.transcript: Labelling handles each node in topological order. Score each ancestor, and put the highest-scoring ones into the candidate cluster up to capacity. l1 is the largest score of a PI inside, l2 the largest score outside plus D. Node i has l1 4 and l2 7, so its label is 7.

slides.title: Every label
slides.alt: Every label: PIs: l = 1; d, e, f, h: 2; g: 3; i, j: 7; k, l: 8; RW’s labels are times, not groups
slides.transcript: Every label: the inputs are 1; d, e, f and h are 2, g is 3; i and j are 7; both outputs are 8. RW’s labels are times, entirely different from the group labels of label propagation.

slides.title: Recovery: working back from the outputs
slides.alt: Recovery: working back from the outputs: Take the candidate clusters of k and l; outside inputs become new roots; 8 clusters in all: k, l, d, e, f, h, b, c; 20 instances; g, j, e, a have 2 each, b and c 3 each; Every instance has complete inputs; Output arrival 8 = the labels
slides.transcript: Recovery works back from the outputs: take the candidate clusters of k and l, and the input nodes outside them become new roots, until no new cluster is needed. That gives 8 clusters and 20 instances, every instance has complete inputs, and both outputs arrive at time 8.

slides.title: What replication buys
slides.alt: What replication buys: With replication: delay 8, 20 instances; Without: exhaustive search over every capacity-legal grouping, best 10; 8 more instances buy 2 units of delay; The optimality result assumes replication is allowed
slides.transcript: With replication the largest delay is 8, using 20 instances. Forbid replication and search every capacity-legal grouping exhaustively, and the best is only 10. Replication trades area for speed, and the paper’s optimality result assumes exactly that replication is allowed.

slides.title: Pseudocode: labelling and recovery
slides.alt: Pseudocode: labelling and recovery: Labelling: topological order; scores, candidate cluster, l1, l2 (Python: rw_label); Recovery: back from the POs; outside inputs become new roots (rw_reconstruct); Instances m@r; +0 inside, +D between; Arrival times: evaluate_instance_delay
slides.transcript: The pseudocode has two parts: labelling computes scores, candidate clusters and labels in topological order; recovery works back from the outputs, making instances for each selected cluster and connecting the instance wires, adding 0 inside a cluster and D between clusters.

slides.title: Limits and open questions
slides.alt: Limits and open questions: The optimality comes from the paper (IEEE TCAD 1995; DAC 1993) and holds only within its model; The 12-node example is a candidate reconstruction; the tie rule is an assumption awaiting the author’s confirmation; This course’s tests check consistency and legal instances; they do not prove optimality
slides.transcript: Finally, the limits: the optimality comes from the paper and holds only within its model. The 12-node example is a candidate reconstruction, and the tie rule is an assumption. This course’s tests only check consistency and legal instances; they do not prove optimality. This submission does not match Lab 09 in the teacher’s catalogue, and the correspondence awaits confirmation.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript: In summary: the goal becomes delay, and each crossing adds D to the path. Labelling gives each node its earliest time, and recovery works back from the outputs to clusters and instances; logic nodes and instances are kept apart, and replication costs area. Finally, go back to the home page and compare the eight modules.
